$comment: Authored port of the hand-written registry group kinesis-records (docs/plans/compat-coverage-modelgen.md §3.11, G6, #1116). One spec in place of five per-language implementations — and of the two that were never written: dotnet-sdk and rust-sdk carry 4 rows each of parity debt for this group, which the port closes. It soaked as kinesis-records-shadow beside those natives until the nightly comparison (run 36113485565) agreed on every one of its 28 (suite, test) pairs in each of three soak runs; the flip then renamed it to kinesis-records, pointed the hand-written registry entry at it and deleted the native code. The clauses are the union of what the five natives asserted — see compat/model/README.md § Authored scenarios. Every record's Data is a blob, so it is written as {"$base64": ...} (#1910): no string literal puts the same bytes on the wire in every backend, which is what parked this port until #2123.

groups.$comment: One one-shard stream, created in setup and deleted in teardown — all five natives create exactly that. The records are put and then read back from the trim horizon of that one shard. The natives disagree on every data literal (go-sdk "record-data", python-sdk "hello-record", node-js-sdk a JSON object, cli "record-1", java-sdk "hello") and on how many records PutRecords sends (go-sdk and cli 2, node-js-sdk 3, python-sdk 5, java-sdk 1); none of them reads its data back, so the choice changes nothing a native observes. This port takes go-sdk's literals throughout — "record-data" under pk1, then r1 under pk1 and r2 under pk2, the last two also exactly what the cli sends — and then asserts the round trip, which no native does. One IR limit is stated rather than hidden: setup cannot poll. Every native waits for the stream to reach ACTIVE before its first test, and a setup step here is one call, so the first test's PutRecord is the one call in this group that may meet a CREATING stream on AWS, which answers ResourceNotFoundException for a stream that is not yet ACTIVE. Overcast creates a stream ACTIVE, so nothing the soak observes depends on it; kinesis-shards states the same limit.
groups.name: kinesis-records

tests.$comment: go-sdk and python-sdk assert a ShardId in the response; node-js-sdk and java-sdk a SequenceNumber; cli nothing. The union is both, non-empty. Both are exported: the ShardId is the shard GetShardIterator reads (python-sdk, node-js-sdk and cli take it from here), and the SequenceNumber is what GetRecords's round trip is checked against. The data is go-sdk's "record-data" under go-sdk's partition key pk1 (also node-js-sdk's and java-sdk's); cli's partition key is the run id, and nothing reads a partition key back in any native.
tests.name: PutRecord

tests.$comment: Every native asserts FailedRecordCount is 0 (python-sdk and go-sdk read an absent count as 0; node-js-sdk, java-sdk and cli require the member). The member is asserted to be present and 0: AWS returns FailedRecordCount on every PutRecords response, and so does Overcast (putRecordsResponse). Two records, go-sdk's and cli's r1/pk1 and r2/pk2 — the most common count, and enough that GetRecords reads a batch rather than a single record. They are read back order-independently, because AWS does not guarantee the order of records within one PutRecords request.
tests.name: PutRecords

tests.$comment: The natives disagree on where the shard comes from: python-sdk, node-js-sdk and cli take PutRecord's ShardId (falling back to shardId-000000000000), go-sdk the first shard of DescribeStream (failing when there is none), java-sdk the first shard of ListShards. The port takes PutRecord's ShardId, which is the shard the record is actually on, and asserts that the stream's shard list contains it — the one-shard stream's only shard, which is what go-sdk's and java-sdk's lookups return. Every native asks for a TRIM_HORIZON iterator and python-sdk, node-js-sdk, java-sdk and cli assert it is non-empty; go-sdk asserts nothing. The iterator is exported for GetRecords.
tests.name: GetShardIterator

tests.$comment: Every native reads with the iterator from GetShardIterator (python-sdk Limit 100, the others 10; this port 10, the majority) and asserts only that Records is non-empty. go-sdk returns success without reading when it has no iterator, and java-sdk fetches one of its own; with the registry's depends the iterator is always there, so neither path is kept. The union is extended by the round trip no native asserts: the records read back are the bytes this scenario put. That is safe to assert because the bytes are the scenario's own — no service-generated value is compared — and it is the claim Kinesis exists to make. Records[0] is PutRecord's record, exactly: one shard, a TRIM_HORIZON iterator, and PutRecord answered before PutRecords was sent, so it has the shard's lowest sequence number; its SequenceNumber equals the one PutRecord returned, its partition key is pk1 and its Data is "record-data". PutRecords's r1 and r2 are found anywhere in the list (AWS does not order records within one PutRecords request), and there is no fourth record. On AWS a record can take a moment to become visible to GetRecords, and a read from TRIM_HORIZON can come back empty with the data behind its NextShardIterator; the natives, which read once, would fail there. So the first read is an `eventually` re-reading the same iterator — valid for five minutes after GetShardIterator issued it — 20 × 500 ms, inside the natives' own waits (3 s to 30 s). Once it has passed, the records are visible and the remaining reads are single.
tests.name: GetRecords
